attributes.comment:
I appreciate the opportunity to comment on FDA’s proposed pilot program for AI-enabled optimization of early-phase clinical trials.

I am the founder of ClearAE, an early-stage AI project focused on safety interpretation in early-phase oncology trials. My comments focus on one proposed use case: AI-assisted interpretation of emerging oncology safety patterns to support dose escalation, dose selection, cohort progression, and sponsor internal go/no-go decisions.

I recommend that FDA include early-phase oncology dose-escalation trials as a priority use case under Category A.1, Scope and Focus. These trials involve small patient populations, high uncertainty, and safety-driven decisions. Clinically meaningful toxicity patterns may emerge through combinations of adverse event timing, CTCAE grade, dose cohort, lab abnormalities, relatedness attribution, and site-level reporting patterns. These patterns may not always appear as obvious serious adverse events at the earliest stage.

AI should not be evaluated only as a tool for real-time data transmission. A high-value use case is AI-assisted safety interpretation, where the system helps medical monitors and safety teams identify weak or emerging toxicity patterns earlier than traditional or manual review, while preserving human oversight.

For Category A.3, Collaboration Models, FDA should consider sponsor, technology vendor, CRO, academic, investigator, and FDA collaboration models. Sensitive clinical trial data should remain within sponsor, CRO, academic, or hospital-approved secure environments where possible. AI developers may not need direct data transfer if analysis can occur within an approved environment and outputs are reviewed at an aggregate or de-identified level.

For Category A.4, Operational Structure, I recommend a staged pilot model:

Retrospective validation using historical or de-identified trial data.
Silent-mode prospective evaluation where AI outputs are generated but do not influence decisions.
Human-in-the-loop prospective use where AI supports, but does not replace, medical monitor and sponsor decision-making.

For Category B.2, Decision Quality, FDA should evaluate whether AI-supported review can identify clinically meaningful safety patterns earlier than traditional/manual review. One practical method is a retrospective “safety replay,” where the system is tested only on data available at each historical point in the trial. FDA and participants could compare when the AI system would have flagged an emerging safety pattern versus when the pattern was identified through traditional review.

For Category B.3, Participant Safety and Data Integrity, relevant metrics should include time from data availability to AI flag, time from flag to human review, false positive rate, false negative rate where assessable, concordance with medical monitor or safety committee assessment, data completeness, and consistency across sites. Earlier detection alone is not sufficient. AI outputs must be clinically meaningful, explainable, and actionable.

For Category B.5, Trustworthiness, AI systems used in early-phase oncology trials should include human oversight, explainable outputs, audit trails, secure data handling, defined intended use, and clear separation between AI-assisted interpretation and final clinical judgment. AI should explain why a pattern was flagged, such as timing, dose relationship, severity, lab abnormality, attribution inconsistency, or cross-site clustering.

In conclusion, I recommend that FDA’s pilot include oncology dose-escalation safety interpretation as a priority AI use case. Real-time trial infrastructure is important, but early-phase oncology also requires better interpretation of emerging safety patterns that may influence dose escalation, cohort progression, dose selection, and early go/no-go decisions.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
